result.note: Both detectors optimize structural modularity, so they tie on the structural corpus. Ariadne's genuine gain is semantic: its embedding edge weighting recovers topics that structure alone cannot, plus a refinement step that guarantees internally connected communities and auto-tuned resolution.

result.independence_caveat: Honest limits on how held-out this is. The first nine cases were written by the same author as the fix and, for the three paraphrase positives, follow the same 'The X for Y is N' against 'Y uses M X' shape as the planted pair with different nouns; the three original negatives are the three guards the implementation's own docstring names. That makes them a regression suite more than an independent sample. The six adversarial cases (N4 through N6, P7 through P9) were written by a reviewer working from the code with the opposite incentive, and four of the six still fail. N7, N8 and N9 came from a SECOND adversarial review and are the most valuable cases here, because they cover the shape the corpus had been missing altogether: two different subjects distinguished by a WORD rather than a numeral. Without them, a relaxation of topic matching measured as free. With them it measures as precision 0.5294, and it was reverted. One change has been made to the comparator in response to this corpus, unit-aware numeric comparison prompted by N4 and P7, and four stative verbs were added to the claim extractor; the rest of what this corpus prompted was measured and rejected.

per_case.why: Two different queues holding different values. The wording is nearly identical to a true contradiction, so this fails if subject identifiers are not required to match.
One subject, two unrelated numeric attributes. This fails if grouping is done on the subject alone without requiring the attribute to match.
The same value stated two different ways. Grouping should pair these, and the comparator should then say nothing, so this checks that the wider grouping did not turn agreement into a false alarm.

The same deadline stated in two units. Before the comparator understood units this was reported as a numeric disagreement of 5 against 5000, which is a false alarm on completely ordinary documentation.

A KNOWN FALSE POSITIVE, kept in the corpus so the published precision counts it. The two statements agree: one states the general budget and the other states the budget on a named path. The comparator sees 5 against 3 and reports a conflict. Detecting that a qualifier scopes a claim needs more than lexical comparison and is not implemented.

A KNOWN FALSE POSITIVE. Both documents say the API is available. One of them happens to contain the word 'no' in an unrelated clause, and the negation signal fires on the asymmetry. The negation test does not check what the negation attaches to.

Contributed by a second adversarial review, and it is the case the corpus was missing entirely. N1 distinguishes its two subjects by a NUMERAL, which the subject-identifier gate rejects before topic matching is ever reached, so until now nothing here tested what happens when two different subjects are distinguished by a WORD. A gateway is not a router and these two statements do not disagree.
Also from the second adversarial review. Upload and download are different limits, not two claims about one limit. One differing word again, and again the two statements are both true.

Also from the second adversarial review. The same attribute on two named components. This is the shape a relaxed topic rule gets wrong most easily, because everything matches except the one word that decides the whole meaning.

per_case.reason: different time values: 30 vs 5 (30.0 vs 5.0 in base units)
per_case.why: Same attribute of the same subject, stated with a different predicate and a different subject phrasing. This is the paraphrase shape the fix targets, in an unrelated domain.

per_case.reason: different size values: 10 vs 25 (10000000.0 vs 25000000.0 in base units)
per_case.why: Paraphrase where the disagreeing statement sits inside a markdown list item rather than a paragraph, so the block segmentation is exercised as well as the grouping.
Containment runs the other way here: the shorter subject belongs to the claim with the longer topic, so the pair is only found if candidate seeding scans from both ends.
Negation across two documents with an identical subject. Covered by the original same-subject-entity route, kept so the fix cannot be shown to have broken it.
Antonym pair across two documents, both of which start with a heading. Before the fix the heading alone was enough to stop any claim being extracted.

A real disagreement the scanner does not see, and the corpus records an attempt to make it see one. The second document uses the verb 'retains'. That verb was added to the claim extractor and is still there, so a claim IS now produced; what still fails is the pairing, because 'retention' and 'records' leave each topic with one token the other lacks. Catching it needed one token of slack in topic matching, which was tried, measured, and reverted: see N7, N8 and N9 for what the slack cost.

per_case.reason: different time values: 30 vs 5 (30.0 vs 300.0 in base units)
per_case.why: A real disagreement written in two different units of the same dimension. Comparing bare numbers reads 30 against 5 and gets the direction of the disagreement wrong; the values have to be converted before they are compared.

Contributed by an adversarial review trying to break the matcher, and it does. One word differs between the two topics ('replica' against 'replicated'), so neither topic contains the other and the paraphrase route never pairs them. Topic containment is lexical; this is what that costs. One token of slack catches it, and was reverted because the same slack reports N7, N8 and N9 as contradictions.

Also from the adversarial review, and the case that settles the argument. The second document says 'a pool of 50 connections' and drops the word 'size' the first document's subject carries. Lexically this is the SAME SHAPE as N7, where a gateway and a router are different subjects: matching tokens everywhere except one word that decides the meaning. No threshold separates P9 from N7, so no relaxation catches this without also inventing that one. It stays a miss, in the denominator.

result.recall_note: Recall is 6 of 9 real disagreements, and precision is 6 of 8 signals returned. The secondary figure restricts the denominator to the 6 cases whose verbs the claim extractor recognises at all, and exists only so a failure of extraction stays distinguishable from a failure of matching. The headline figures are the unrestricted ones. Nothing is excluded to improve either number: every miss and every false positive is in the corpus, labelled, and counted. Recall reaching 1.0 does not mean the scanner is complete; it means this corpus no longer contains a disagreement it misses, and three of those cases stopped being misses because the scanner was changed in response to them. See independence_caveat.

why.advisory: The scanner is lexical and over-approximate. It groups claims whose topics nest and whose subject identifiers match, then applies a numeric, negation, or antonym test. It is not an entailment model, and its output is a prompt for a human, not a finding.
why.held_out: Every case is in a domain absent from the planted token-cost corpus. One change HAS been made to the comparator in response to these cases, unit-aware numeric comparison prompted by N4 and P7, and four stative verbs were added to the claim extractor after P6; those are general rules rather than patches shaped around one sentence, but the corpus prompted them and saying it did not would be untrue. Everything else this corpus prompted was measured and REJECTED. One token of slack in topic matching takes recall from 6 of 9 to 9 of 9 and was reverted, because with N7, N8 and N9 present it takes precision from 0.75 to 0.5294. Those three cases were added by the review that found it.
known_limitations: Claim extraction recognises fifteen shallow verb patterns. A disagreement stated with any other verb produces no claim and cannot be detected, whatever the grouping does. Widening the set is cheap and does not make the extractor any less shallow.

The original same-subject-entity route compares any two claims with the same subject entity and the same predicate. Two unrelated numeric facts stated that way (for example 'X has 3 replicas' and 'X has 5 workers') will still raise a signal. That route predates this work and is unchanged.

Topic matching is lexical. Two claims that share vocabulary without sharing meaning can be grouped, and two paraphrases with no shared vocabulary are never grouped. The one token of slack that catches a paraphrase differing by a single word necessarily also loosens the rule in the other direction; it did not cost precision on this corpus, which is one corpus and not a guarantee.
why.recall_denominator: All cases labelled a real disagreement, including the three the scanner does not see. Nothing is excluded from the denominator to raise the number, and the two known false positives stay in the precision denominator for the same reason.
why.why_recall_is_not_higher: It could be, and the cost was measured rather than guessed. P9 is 'the connection pool size' against 'a pool of 50 connections in the payment service'. N7 is 'the cache size for the gateway' against 'the cache size for the router'. Lexically those are the same shape: every token matches except one, and that one decides whether the two statements disagree. Any threshold that catches P9 reports N7, so the choice is not between a better and a worse matcher but between missing three real disagreements and inventing three that are not there. A scanner whose output is advisory has to be worth reading; at precision 0.5294 it is not. Separating them needs entailment, which this is not.

why.baseline_definition: strong = grep the corpus for the query terms, rank files by match count, read the top 12 whole. Same question, same corpus, same tokenizer as the graph route. The budget is the shared default in common.py and was not changed for this task.
why.determinism: Changed symbols are hard-coded, every key list is sorted, the packer orders by (required, score, key), and no sampling is used.
limitations: This corpus is close to the worst case for node-level slicing. Every impacted symbol is two lines long and every impacted file contains nothing but impacted symbols, so a whole-file read wastes almost no tokens and the per-unit label the graph must emit (# kind canonical) is a large fraction of each unit's cost.

The recorded impact set is exactly the set of textual callers of the gateway, and those callers all name it literally. Grep is therefore near-optimal at finding them, which is not true of real codebases with indirect dispatch, re-exports, or renamed imports.
Reverse reachability is structural and over-approximate. It returns more nodes than the recorded impact set, and the extras are paid for in tokens.

Correctness is containment of required symbol names, not an assessment of whether a review written from the context would be any good. A route can contain a name without the reviewer being able to reason about it.

contradiction_machinery_diagnosis.stage_1_extraction: Every planted document opens with a markdown heading. Claim extraction segments markdown blocks before splitting sentences, so the heading is its own block and the sentence beneath it is read. 6 of 6 pairs yield a claim on both sides. Before that segmentation existed the count here was zero.
contradiction_machinery_diagnosis.stage_2_comparability: The two sides are phrased differently: the runbook says 'the cache TTL for service N is ...' and the architecture note says 'service N uses ...', so neither the subject nor the predicate matches literally. They are grouped by the paraphrase route instead, which requires the subject identifiers to be equal and one claim's topic to contain the other's. 6 of 6 pairs are judged comparable. Under the original exact (subject_id, predicate) rule the count was zero.

why.correctness_rule: Per pair, a route is correct only if both document names and both values (with their unit) appear in what it retrieved. Deterministic substring containment, aggregated with contains_all. No model judges anything. Document names in the graph route come from the graph's own source records, so a route cannot get credit for a document its evidence did not come from.
why.graph_definition: graph = ingest the corpus, extract claims, run dkg.evidence.contradiction.find_contradictions, and return exactly the chunks dkg.context.provenance.claim_evidence_bounded records as supporting the two contradicting claims. Nothing is hand-coded and no answer is supplied from the ground truth.
limitations: The planted contradictions sit in twelve very small markdown files whose text is dominated by the query terms, so grep ranking puts all twelve at the top and the strong baseline sees both sides of every pair for a few hundred tokens. This corpus is close to the best case for a grep baseline and the worst case for arguing that retrieval cost matters; a larger document corpus with many near-miss files would be a harder and more informative test.

graph_evidence_oracle is a diagnostic, not a route. Its chunks are selected by an oracle that already knows which two documents disagree, so it shows only what the evidence path would have cost had detection worked. It is excluded from every savings figure.
The naive and strong aggregates charge one retrieval per question. single_pass_tokens reports the batched alternative for all routes.
Only the document plane is exercised. The 414 code files are ingested with format code:python, for which the document claim extractor is deliberately skipped, so they contribute no claims.
why.naive_definition: naive = every file in the corpus, concatenated. It is the labelled upper bound and not a serious opponent: to find a contradiction this way you must read everything.

why.baseline_definition: strong = grep-ranked top files read whole, at the shared STRONG_BASELINE_FILE_BUDGET of 12 files from common.py, using the same question text the graph route gets. The budget was taken as given and was not adjusted in this task, in either direction. strong_at_parity is a separate supplementary figure: the smallest prefix of the same grep ranking that reaches full recall. It is reported so the equal-correctness cost is visible, and it is not substituted for the primary baseline.
why.corpus_size: 414 code files and 20 doc files (248560 plus 3497 bytes), generated deterministically by tests/code/corpus/large/generate_corpus.py. Ground truth is known by construction: 8 layer gateways with 300 impacted symbols each.
limitations: The graph route costs more raw tokens than the strong baseline on this corpus. The strong baseline reaches roughly a quarter of the required set within its file budget, so it is cheap because it is incomplete, not because it is efficient. Compare it to strong_at_parity before concluding anything about efficiency.

The exact answer is over-approximate. It returns more symbols than ground truth names, because the structural code graph resolves references by name and also carries module nodes and the class method on the call path. Recall is complete; precision is reported per seed as precision_vs_ground_truth and is below 1.0.

The corpus is synthetic and regularly layered, so grep ranking behaves unusually cleanly on it: the top-ranked files are all genuinely relevant. On real code the strong baseline would waste more of its budget, which means this comparison flatters the baseline rather than the graph.
Only the input-token cost of the context is measured. Neither route is executed against a model, so nothing here measures answer quality beyond required-set recall, and no output tokens are counted.
The naive route's token count is identical for every seed by construction, since it is the whole corpus; only its correctness varies.

why.scoring: Correctness is recall against the ground-truth required set, never a model judgement. The text routes are scored on the bare symbol name, because the canonical form never appears in source and scoring them on it would score them zero for text they genuinely read; that choice favours the baseline. The graph route is scored on the canonical keys in its exact answer list. The required set was not shrunk for any route.
why.token_budget: The graph route's supporting pack is held to 2000 tokens for every seed. The value was fixed before measuring and is not tuned per seed or against the baseline.

result.verdict: Yes: the graph route beat the strong baseline, using 4088 tokens against the baseline's 10144 (2.48x cheaper) while scoring 1.0 on the specified correctness check against the baseline's 1.0, and 1.0 against 1.0 on the strict evidence check. Read the strict check, not the loose one: the baseline passed the loose check on 0 of 8 questions purely because a bare digit turned up in unrelated numbered source code, having never retrieved the note that holds the answer. Grep-ranking 'retry budget layer' over this corpus returns the layer source files, whose many occurrences of 'layer' outrank the one prose note that says what the retry budget is.

why.baseline_definition: The strong baseline is what a competent agent without a graph does: grep the corpus for the question's terms, rank all 434 files by match count, and read the top 12 in full. It gets the same corpus and the same question the graph route gets, and the shared file budget from common.py, unchanged. Nothing was tuned to make it lose.

capabilities.note: Both optional arms are capability-detected. With neither present, hybrid search degrades to keyword-plus-FTS RRF, which on this corpus still returns the answer-bearing note inside the retrieval limit but in file order rather than by relevance. Measured in that degraded configuration the graph route scores 0.875 strict rather than 1.0: neither lexical arm can tell 'layer 7' from 'layer 3', because both tokenizers drop single characters, so the last-ranked note is the one the budget drops. That is the honest floor.

why.correctness: Two checks, both from ground truth. The primary 'correctness' is the specified one: contains_all over answer_contains against the text the route retrieved. 'evidence_correctness' is strict: the route must have actually retrieved the document ground truth names as holding the answer, and the answer string must be present in what it returned.
why.determinism: Questions are sorted, retrieved documents are sorted, and packing is ordered by (required, score, key). No randomness anywhere in the task.
why.graph_route: The whole corpus is ingested into one throwaway graph (docs as markdown, code forced through the plain-text reader), retrieved with hybrid search at limit 8, and packed by pack_units into a 512-token budget. Unit scores come from the search rank, so the pack reproduces the retrieval order. No unit is marked structurally required: marking the ground-truth document required would be handing the graph the answer.
limitations: The specified correctness check is much weaker than it looks. answer_contains is a bare digit ('3' through '10'), and a corpus of four hundred numbered modules contains the low digits many times over, so a route can pass it on text that has nothing to do with the question. That is exactly what the strong baseline does on the low-numbered layers. The strict evidence check is reported for that reason. Neither check was weakened, and the loose one is still the headline 'correctness' field.

The graph route's perfect strict score depends on the optional embedding and reranker arms being pre-staged. They are capability-detected, and the run records which were active under why.capabilities. Measured with both arms switched off, the graph route scores 0.875 strict instead of 1.0, because neither lexical arm can distinguish 'layer 7' from 'layer 3' and the last-ranked note is the one the budget drops. The published 1.0 is the with-models figure, not a universal one.

Code files are ingested through the plain-text reader, so the code plane's symbol graph plays no part in this task. That is honest for prose question answering and means this result says nothing about code questions.
Eight questions of one shape (a numeric fact stated in one note) is a narrow sample. The absolute ratio should not be read as a general figure.
The naive route is an upper bound, not a competitor. Beating it proves nothing.

pricing.note: Costs are input-token costs at these rates on this date. The price table is configuration, not a measurement: rates change and vary by tier and provider. The measurement is the token count; substitute your own rate and redo the multiplication.

why.same_haystack: Both routes search the same 434 files. The graph route indexes 885 chunks, of which only 20 come from the 20 prose documents, so the code files are real noise in the retrieval task rather than excluded to flatter the result.
why.task: Eight ground-truth questions, each answerable from exactly one prose note in the corpus. Ground truth is known by construction from the corpus generator, not labelled by hand and not judged by a model.

tokenizer.note: Both sides of every comparison are counted by the same function, so a ratio never mixes a tokenizer count with an estimate. When the real tokenizer is absent the fallback estimator is used and this field says so.

knowledge_base_qa.title: Question answering over documents and code

tokenizer.note: Both sides of every comparison are counted by the same function, so a ratio never mixes a tokenizer count with an estimate. When the real tokenizer is absent the fallback estimator is used and this field says so.

why.correctness: recall against a required set known by construction. Never an LLM judge. A route that saves tokens by answering less scores lower and the saving is not reported as a win.
why.limitation: The corpus is generated and regular, which flatters grep: its files are small and saturated with the query terms, so the strong baseline ranks near-optimally. Real code with indirect dispatch, re-exports, and renamed imports would be harder for it.
why.naive_baseline: the whole corpus, an upper bound only; nobody competent works this way
why.strong_baseline: a competent agent without a graph: grep the corpus for the query terms, rank files by match count, read the top files whole. This is the baseline that matters.

token_cost.title: Token cost across four tasks (strong baseline)

estimator.kind: in-repo deterministic estimator, not a vendor tokenizer
estimator.note: Both sides of every comparison use this estimator, so the ratio is substantially independent of it. Character counts and the character ratio are published so that can be verified.
estimator.rule: runs of up to four letters, single digits, newlines, and single non-alphanumeric characters each count as one token; other whitespace is not counted

why.headline: The figure to quote is token_ratio_vs_graph_plus_sources, which charges the graph route for reading the files its answer names. The answer-only ratio is reported for completeness and flatters the graph route by assuming no code is read at all.
why.limitation: Answer quality is not measured here, only size. The accuracy of the underlying analyses is measured separately, and those analyses are structural and over-approximate.
why.scope: Measured on this corpus only. The ratio scales with corpus size: the full-corpus cost grows with the repository while a graph answer stays bounded by what the question touches. This is not a universal claim and must not be quoted as one.
